subject: rat
title: What If a City Paid a Bounty for Every Rat Tail? Hanoi Did in 1902

scenes.text: What if a city paid cash for every rat tail? Hanoi did, and got more rats.
1902. French-ruled Hanoi has brand-new sewers, and rats are climbing out of the toilets. The fear is plague.
First the city sends rat catchers into the sewers. By June they report over ten thousand kills a day. On June 21: 20,112.
It still isn't enough. So the city offers everyone one cent per rat. As proof, just bring in the tail.
Soon officials notice live rats running around with no tails. People were cutting them off and letting the rats go to breed.
Then inspectors find rat farms on the edge of town. The bounty is scrapped. In 1906, plague kills at least 263 people.

description:
What if a city paid a bounty for every rat tail? Colonial Hanoi tried it in 1902.
With rats spreading through the new French-built sewers and plague feared, the city first hired rat catchers, who reported 20,112 kills on 21 June 1902 alone, and then offered the public one cent per tail. People began cutting off tails and releasing the rats to breed, smuggling rats in from outside, and even farming them. The scheme was cancelled; a plague outbreak in 1906 killed at least 263 people. Historian Michael Vann uncovered the story, now a standard example of a perverse incentive.

first_comment: Economists call this the cobra effect; the historian who found the file says it should be the rat effect. Which reward scheme have you seen backfire?
